messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Petra's Story

Petra was thirty-nine when the diagnosis came through—stage three ovarian cancer, caught late enough that the surgical team spoke in careful, measured tones about "aggressive treatment protocols" and "realistic expectations." She had been a dentist for fourteen years, meticulous with her hands, confident in her ability to read what a mouth could tell her. The irony was not lost on her: she had spent her career examining other people's bodies for signs of disease, and her own body had betrayed her in silence. The surgery came first—a hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, followed by six months of chemotherapy that left her nauseated, bald, and staring at a stranger in the mirror. By the time she finished treatment, the cancer was in remission, but Petra was not.

The hospital smell—that particular blend of bleach, antiseptic, and something else she could never quite name—had become a trigger that sent her into a spiral of dread. When she returned to her practice three months after finishing chemo, she found that the faint chemical scent in her own office, a residue from the cleaning supplies in the sterilization room, could unsettle her for hours. More insidiously, old photographs began to trigger the same cascade of panic. She had discovered a picture from five years ago—herself at a friend's wedding, radiant and whole—and the sight of that version of herself, the one before the diagnosis, before the surgery, before the poison they pumped into her veins, crystallized something terrible: she was not that person anymore. That woman was gone. What remained was someone fundamentally compromised, someone whose body could no longer be trusted. The certainty of this belief had the weight of truth. She was weak—weak for getting sick, weak for struggling through treatment, weak for not being able to simply move on the way everyone seemed to expect her to. And the more she dwelled on those old photographs, the more convinced she became that the damage was permanent, that no amount of time would restore what she had lost.

The conviction that she had permanently changed for the worse, that her body was now unreliable and dangerous, led her to withdraw from the very relationships that might have sustained her. Her partner, Marcus, had been supportive through treatment, but Petra found herself unable to let him touch her. She avoided looking at her own body—the surgical scars, the way her abdomen felt different, the lingering fatigue that no amount of rest seemed to cure. Showering became an ordeal she rushed through with her eyes closed. At work, she began finding reasons to cancel appointments, telling her office manager that she needed to reduce her schedule, that she wasn't quite ready to return to full capacity. What she didn't say was that the thought of being confined in the dental chair—trapped in that position, unable to move, dependent on the patient to remain still—had become unbearable. The feeling of entrapment, of having no options, no escape route, no control, sent her into a state of suffocating anxiety that she couldn't explain to anyone.

She stopped talking about the cancer altogether. When colleagues asked how she was doing, she gave brief, deflecting answers. With Marcus, she refused to discuss her fears, her body's limitations, or the dark thoughts that sometimes visited her at three in the morning. The isolation deepened her conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with her, that she was broken in a way that couldn't be shared or understood. Her avoidance of other people—the way she had begun declining social invitations, making excuses to stay home—only reinforced her sense of weakness and permanent damage. The less she allowed herself to be seen, the more real the belief became that she was no longer the person worth knowing. By the time she called a therapist, six months into remission, Petra had constructed a prison of her own making, one built from the conviction that her body had failed her and that she herself was fundamentally, irreparably changed.
